questions.prompt: Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle θ, using the unit circle?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle θ, using the unit circle?

choices.text: On the unit circle sin θ + cos θ = 1 for every angle θ, because the coordinates of a point add to the radius; squaring both sides gives sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
The point at angle θ is (sin θ, cos θ), so sin θ + cos θ = 1.
For θ = 30°: (1/2)² + (√3/2)² = 1, so the identity holds.
The point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), and every point on the unit circle satisfies x² + y² = 1; substituting gives cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

questions.correct_answer: The point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), and every point on the unit circle satisfies x² + y² = 1; substituting gives cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
questions.grading_note: The coordinates of the point satisfy the circle equation. The others check one angle or rely on the false statement sin θ + cos θ = 1.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs a and b, hypotenuse c, and acute angle θ opposite a. Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1?
questions.prompt_markup: A right triangle has legs a and b, hypotenuse c, and acute angle θ opposite a. Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1?

choices.text: sin θ = a/c and cos θ = b/c, so sin²θ + cos²θ = (a + b)²/c², and (a + b)² = c² by the Pythagorean Theorem, so the sum is 1.
sin θ = b/c and cos θ = a/c, so sin θ + cos θ = (a + b)/c = 1.
sin θ = a/c and cos θ = b/c, so sin²θ + cos²θ = (a² + b²)/c² = c²/c² = 1 by the Pythagorean Theorem.
In a 3-4-5 triangle, (3/5)² + (4/5)² = 1, so the identity holds.

questions.correct_answer: sin θ = a/c and cos θ = b/c, so sin²θ + cos²θ = (a² + b²)/c² = c²/c² = 1 by the Pythagorean Theorem.
questions.grading_note: Both ratios and a² + b² = c². The others swap the ratios and use a + b = c, square a sum incorrectly, or check one triangle.

questions.prompt: Which argument proves 1 + tan²θ = 1/cos²θ wherever cos θ ≠ 0?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument proves 1 + tan²θ = 1/cos²θ wherever cos θ ≠ 0?

choices.text: Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by sin²θ to get 1 + cos²θ/sin²θ = 1/sin²θ; since cos²θ/sin²θ = tan²θ, this gives 1 + tan²θ = 1/cos²θ.
For θ = 0: 1 + 0 = 1/1, so the identity holds.
Square tan θ = sin θ/cos θ to get tan²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ = 1/cos²θ.
Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ, which is allowed because cos θ ≠ 0: sin²θ/cos²θ + 1 = 1/cos²θ, and sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.

questions.correct_answer: Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ, which is allowed because cos θ ≠ 0: sin²θ/cos²θ + 1 = 1/cos²θ, and sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.
questions.grading_note: Divide the Pythagorean identity by cos²θ. The others divide by sin²θ and then treat cos²θ/sin²θ as tan²θ (it is 1/tan²θ), replace sin²θ by 1, or check one angle.

questions.prompt: θ is in quadrant II, and its point on the unit circle is (x, y) with x < 0 < y. Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 with a reference triangle?
questions.prompt_markup: θ is in quadrant II, and its point on the unit circle is (x, y) with x < 0 < y. Which argument proves sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 with a reference triangle?

choices.text: The reference triangle has legs x and y, so x + y = 1, which means cos θ + sin θ = 1.
The reference triangle has legs |x| and |y| and hypotenuse 1, so |x|² + |y|² = 1. Squaring removes the signs, so x² + y² = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
The legs of the reference triangle are x and y, and x is negative in quadrant II, so x² + y² = -1 there, which means cos²θ + sin²θ = -1 instead of 1.
The identity was proved for acute angles, so it is true in quadrant II with no further work.

questions.correct_answer: The reference triangle has legs |x| and |y| and hypotenuse 1, so |x|² + |y|² = 1. Squaring removes the signs, so x² + y² = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
questions.grading_note: Side lengths are |x| and |y|; squares remove the signs. The others add the legs, mishandle the negative coordinate, or skip the argument.

For θ = 0: (0 + 1)² = 1 + 0, so the identity holds.
(sin θ + cos θ)² = 1² = 1 because sin θ + cos θ = 1.

questions.prompt: Which argument proves sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = sin²θ - cos²θ?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument proves sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = sin²θ - cos²θ?

choices.text: Divide both sides by sin²θ - cos²θ to get sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, which is the Pythagorean identity, so the identity is true.
sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = (sin θ - cos θ)⁴, which equals sin²θ - cos²θ.
For θ = π/4 both sides are 0, so the identity holds.
sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ) = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(1) = sin²θ - cos²θ.

questions.correct_answer: sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ) = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(1) = sin²θ - cos²θ.
questions.grading_note: Factor as a difference of squares and use the Pythagorean identity. The others assume the identity (and divide by an expression that can be 0), use the false rule a⁴ - b⁴ = (a - b)⁴, or check one angle.

questions.prompt: Which argument proves (1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = sin²θ?
questions.prompt_markup: Which argument proves (1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = sin²θ?

choices.text: For θ = π/2: (1 - 0)(1 + 0) = 1 = sin²(π/2), so the identity holds.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - 2cos θ + cos²θ, and by the Pythagorean identity this equals sin²θ.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ, and 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ by the Pythagorean identity.
(1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 + cos²θ, which equals sin²θ.

questions.correct_answer: (1 - cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ, and 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ by the Pythagorean identity.
questions.grading_note: Multiply (difference of squares), then use the identity. The others multiply incorrectly or check one angle.

questions.prompt: Which argument proves cos²θ - sin²θ = 2cos²θ - 1?

choices.text: Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1.
Add sin²θ to both sides to get cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1 + sin²θ, which is always true.
For θ = 0: 1 - 0 = 2 - 1, so the identity holds.
Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - 1 - cos²θ = -1, so the identity is false for every θ.

questions.correct_answer: Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ: cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ = 2cos²θ - 1.
questions.grading_note: Substitute sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ and subtract the whole expression. The others drop the parentheses, check one angle, or end with an unproved statement.
